title: Certified Payroll in Massachusetts: Prevailing Wage and Reporting Requirements
summary: Massachusetts certified payroll and prevailing wage requirements for contractors on public projects, covering reporting deadlines, penalties, and compliance.
body_markdown:
Massachusetts enforces some of the strictest prevailing wage rules in the country, and the certified payroll reporting requirements that come with them leave little room for error. The state's prevailing wage law is a strict liability statute, meaning contractors face penalties even when a violation was unintentional. For trade contractors working on public projects across the Commonwealth, understanding what the law requires, how to report accurately, and what happens when reporting falls short is not optional.


The Massachusetts Prevailing Wage Law, codified in[M.G.L. c. 149, §§ 26–27D](https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartI/TitleXXI/Chapter149/Section27) , applies to all public construction work, including additions and alterations to public buildings, soil explorations, test borings, and demolition. Two state agencies share responsibility: the[Department of Labor Standards (DLS)](https://www.mass.gov/orgs/department-of-labor-standards) administers and interprets the law, while the Attorney General's Fair Labor Division enforces it.


## **What the Massachusetts Prevailing Wage Law Covers**


The scope of the law is broader than many contractors expect. Understanding which projects trigger prevailing wage obligations, and which workers are covered, prevents compliance failures before they start.


### **Covered Projects and Workers**


Every public construction project in Massachusetts requires prevailing wage payments, regardless of the dollar amount or whether the project must be competitively bid. The law covers state government construction, municipal projects, county projects, public school construction, and road, bridge, and infrastructure work.


Prevailing wages must be paid to all covered employees, whether they work for the general contractor, a filed sub-bidder, or any subcontractor on the project. The law applies equally to union and non-union employers. Apprentices working on prevailing wage projects must be registered with the DLS Division of Apprentice Standards and must carry an apprentice identification card on the jobsite.


### **Wage Rates and Fringe Benefits**


Before soliciting bids, the awarding authority must obtain a prevailing wage rate schedule from DLS. The schedule specifies hourly rates and fringe benefit rates for each job classification on the project. Key rules around wage rates include:


-


**Rate validity:** Prevailing wage rates remain in effect for 90 days from the date of issue. Projects not bid within that window require a new rate request.


-


**Multi-year projects:** For construction lasting more than one year, contractors must obtain updated wage rate schedules and pay no less than the updated rates. All scheduled wage increases listed must be paid on the specified effective dates.


-


**Overtime:** Workers who exceed 40 hours in a workweek must be paid 1.5 times the base hourly rate plus the full fringe benefit amount for every overtime hour.


-


**Fringe benefit credits:** Only contributions to bona fide health and welfare, pension, or supplemental unemployment plans may be credited toward the fringe benefit portion of the prevailing wage. Vacation time, sick time, workers' compensation, and unemployment insurance do not qualify as creditable fringe benefits under Massachusetts law.


The prevailing wage rate schedule must be posted in a visible location at the construction site.


## **Certified Payroll Reporting Requirements**


Certified payroll is the primary mechanism Massachusetts uses to verify that contractors are paying workers correctly on public projects. The reporting obligations fall on every contractor and subcontractor performing work on a covered project.


### **What the Reports Must Include**


Under[M.G.L. c. 149, § 27B](https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartI/TitleXXI/Chapter149/Section27) , all contractors and subcontractors must submit weekly certified payroll reports directly to the awarding authority. Each report must document:


-


Worker names, job classifications, and hours worked per day


-


Hourly wage rates and fringe benefit amounts paid


-


Gross wages and deductions


-


A signed statement of compliance certifying that the contractor has paid the correct prevailing wage rates and benefits


Reports are due no later than the week following the pay period they cover. Both the general contractor and every subcontractor on the project must submit their own reports independently. General contractors are also responsible for collecting and monitoring their subcontractors' certified payroll submissions to confirm alignment with ​[prevailing wage compliance](https://www.buildtrayd.com/solution/compliance/certified-payroll) requirements.


### **OSHA 10 Training Documentation**


Beyond payroll reporting, Massachusetts requires all employees working on public construction projects to complete OSHA 10-hour construction safety training. Workers must carry documentation of their OSHA 10 certification while on the jobsite. Contractors should verify OSHA 10 compliance as part of ​[workforce onboarding](https://www.buildtrayd.com/products/hr-people-management/construction-worker-onboarding) for any crew assigned to a public project.


## **Penalties for Non-Compliance**


Massachusetts treats prevailing wage violations seriously, and the Attorney General's Fair Labor Division has a well-documented track record of enforcement.


### **Financial Consequences**


The prevailing wage law is a strict liability statute. Contractors who fail to pay the correct rates or submit accurate certified payroll records face penalties regardless of whether the underpayment was intentional. Consequences include:


-


**Back wages and restitution** owed to affected workers for the full amount of underpayment.


-


**Civil citations and fines** assessed by the Attorney General's Office. The AG's Fair Labor Division assessed more than $2.7 million in restitution and penalties against 66 construction companies in a single year, according to enforcement data published by the[Massachusetts Attorney General's Office](https://www.mass.gov/orgs/office-of-the-attorney-general) .


-


**Debarment** from bidding on, contracting with, or working on public construction projects in Massachusetts. Debarment periods have ranged from 18 months to 10 years in documented enforcement actions.


### **Common Violations**


The most frequently cited violations on Massachusetts public projects include failure to pay the prevailing wage, failure to submit true and accurate certified payroll records, failure to register and properly pay apprentices, and misclassifying workers into lower-paid job classifications. Even submitting incomplete reports with missing classifications, wage data, or fringe information creates compliance exposure that may surface during an audit.


## **How to Stay Compliant on Massachusetts Public Projects**


Consistent compliance on prevailing wage projects requires operational discipline across[construction payroll](https://www.buildtrayd.com/products/payroll/construction-payroll) processing, record-keeping, and field coordination. The following practices reduce the risk of costly violations.


### **Match Payroll to the Wage Rate Schedule**


Every payroll run on a public project must reference the specific prevailing wage rate schedule issued for that project. Rates vary by trade classification and project, so applying a generic rate or carrying over rates from a previous project can result in underpayment. When projects last more than a year, contractors must obtain updated schedules and adjust wages accordingly.


### **Maintain Clean Records Across the Workforce**


Accurate ​[field and labor tracking](https://www.buildtrayd.com/products/field/construction-worker-app) is the foundation of compliant certified payroll. Every worker's hours, classification, and jobsite assignment must be captured daily. When crew members move between public and private projects, or between multiple public projects with different wage schedules, separating hours by project and applying the correct rate for each is critical.


### **Coordinate Subcontractor Compliance**


General contractors bear responsibility for monitoring their subcontractors' certified payroll submissions. A missed or inaccurate report from a subcontractor creates liability for the general contractor as well. Collecting, reviewing, and archiving subcontractor certified payroll records weekly, alongside ​[payroll reports](https://www.buildtrayd.com/products/payroll/construction-payroll-reports) from your own workforce, keeps the project audit-ready.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### Who must submit certified payroll reports in Massachusetts?


Every contractor and subcontractor performing work on a public construction project in Massachusetts must submit weekly certified payroll reports directly to the awarding authority.


### How often are Massachusetts certified payroll reports due?


Reports must be submitted weekly, no later than the week following the pay period they cover.


### Does the Massachusetts prevailing wage law apply to all public projects?


Yes. The law applies to every public construction project in Massachusetts regardless of the dollar amount of the contract or whether competitive bidding was required.


### What happens if a contractor submits inaccurate certified payroll records?


The Attorney General's Fair Labor Division can issue civil citations, require restitution and back wages to affected workers, and debar the contractor from future public construction work in Massachusetts.


### Are apprentices covered by Massachusetts prevailing wage requirements?


Yes. Apprentices on public construction projects must be registered with the DLS Division of Apprentice Standards and must be paid according to the approved apprentice wage schedule for their classification.


### Do workers on Massachusetts public projects need OSHA 10 training?


Yes. All employees working on public construction projects in Massachusetts must complete the OSHA 10-hour construction safety training and carry proof of certification on the jobsite.
